title: One-to-one (1:1)
summary: Each parent pairs with at most one child — usually a UNIQUE FK.

example.sql: account_id INTEGER UNIQUE NOT NULL REFERENCES lab_accounts(id)

exercise.prompt: Each user has at most one profile: lab_l06_profiles.user_id → lab_l06_users.id, UNIQUE and NOT NULL.
exercise.hint: 1:1 = a foreign key + a UNIQUE constraint on it.

exercise.solution:
from sqlalchemy import String, Integer, Numeric, Boolean, ForeignKey, UniqueConstraint, create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class LabL06User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "lab_l06_users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(120))


class LabL06Profile(Base):
    __tablename__ = "lab_l06_profiles"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200))
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("lab_l06_users.id"), unique=True)

engine = create_engine(DATABASE_URL)
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)

body:
Each parent pairs with at most one child — usually a UNIQUE FK.

Why it matters: Profiles, settings, and credentials often share a 1:1 with a user/account. Without UNIQUE on the FK, the database silently allows multiple children (accidental 1:N).

SQL ↔ ORM: UNIQUE FK ↔ Prisma @unique on the FK field ↔ SQL UNIQUE.
why: Profiles, settings, and credentials often share a 1:1 with a user/account. Without UNIQUE on the FK, the database silently allows multiple children (accidental 1:N).
objectives: Implement 1:1 with a UNIQUE foreign key on the dependent table.
Explain how UNIQUE changes cardinality vs plain 1:N.
pitfalls: Forgetting UNIQUE — tests may pass until duplicate inserts appear.
Shared primary key 1:1 is valid but harder to migrate; labs prefer UNIQUE FK.
mappingNotes: UNIQUE FK ↔ Prisma @unique on the FK field ↔ SQL UNIQUE.
teachAlong: Cause: each account may have only one profile.
